reference.source: Standard haematopoietic cell transplantation and transplant immunology reference texts
clinicalPearls: Develops later after allogeneic transplantation and is characterised by fibrosis and features resembling autoimmune connective-tissue disease rather than the acute inflammatory pattern
Diagnosis now rests on characteristic clinical features regardless of the interval since transplant, and it may overlap with persisting acute disease
Skin manifestations range from lichen-planus-like eruptions to sclerodermatous change with tightening, fibrosis, and restricted movement
Sicca features are common, with dry eyes and a dry mouth accompanied by oral lichenoid change and ulceration
Multiple organs may be affected, including the lungs with bronchiolitis obliterans, the liver, the gut and oesophagus, the joints and fascia, and the genital mucosa
Prior acute graft-versus-host disease is the strongest risk factor, and the condition is a leading cause of late morbidity and non-relapse mortality
Management is prolonged immunosuppression combining corticosteroids with calcineurin inhibitors and steroid-sparing agents, alongside organ-specific supportive care
Vigilant infection prophylaxis is essential because prolonged immunosuppression and functional asplenia markedly increase infection risk
reference.pathophysiology: Alloreactive donor T cells, together with dysregulated B-cell responses and autoantibody formation, sustain chronic immune-mediated inflammation. Damage to the thymus impairs the development of tolerance, allowing autoreactive and alloreactive clones to persist. Ongoing inflammation drives progressive tissue fibrosis across multiple organs, producing a phenotype that resembles scleroderma and other autoimmune connective-tissue diseases rather than the acute epithelial injury of acute graft-versus-host disease.
additionalDifferentials: Scleroderma or systemic sclerosis and other connective-tissue diseases
Nutritional deficiency causing skin and mucosal change
additionalInvestigations: Clinical scoring of organ involvement to establish the diagnosis and grade severity
Skin or mucosal biopsy in atypical presentations
Pulmonary function tests and imaging for suspected bronchiolitis obliterans
Ophthalmic assessment including tear-production testing for ocular sicca
Liver function tests with biopsy where needed
Oesophageal and gut evaluation for strictures or dysmotility
Screening for and monitoring of opportunistic infection
redFlags: New airflow obstruction or bronchiolitis obliterans indicating serious pulmonary disease
Progressive sclerosis with joint contractures and impaired function
Severe weight loss and malnutrition from gut or oesophageal involvement
Serious or recurrent infection during immunosuppression
Features suggesting disease relapse or a secondary malignancy
reference.prognosis: The course is variable: limited disease may resolve, whereas extensive sclerodermatous or pulmonary disease causes long-term disability and contributes to non-relapse mortality; an associated graft-versus-tumour effect can reduce the risk of underlying disease relapse.
pitfalls: Waiting for an arbitrary time cut-off rather than diagnosing on characteristic features
Missing bronchiolitis obliterans because early lung disease is often asymptomatic
Neglecting infection prophylaxis during prolonged immunosuppression
Under-treating ocular and oral sicca and allowing avoidable complications
Overlooking the increased risk of secondary malignancy on long-term follow-up
references: Consensus diagnostic and scoring criteria for chronic graft-versus-host disease
Standard haematopoietic cell transplantation reference texts
management: Systemic corticosteroids, often combined with a calcineurin inhibitor, as first-line immunosuppression
Second-line therapy for steroid-refractory disease using ruxolitinib, extracorporeal photopheresis, ibrutinib, mycophenolate or rituximab
Organ-directed treatment including topical corticosteroids and calcineurin inhibitors for cutaneous and oral disease, ocular lubricants for sicca, and inhaled therapy for bronchiolitis obliterans
Infection prophylaxis against bacteria, fungi, viruses and Pneumocystis during prolonged immunosuppression
Surveillance and supportive care for organ complications, with pulmonary function monitoring, physiotherapy for sclerosis and fasciitis, and nutritional and ophthalmic support
Multidisciplinary transplant, dermatology, ophthalmology and respiratory input, with a slow immunosuppression taper guided by response
